newsitem.title: INDIA: India Reliance focuses on debt financing.
newsitem.headline: India Reliance focuses on debt financing.

text.p: Reliance Industries, India's largest private firm, will continue to finance its huge capacity expansions through debt, analysts said on Thursday.

"The focus of the future will be on debt financing," said a petrochemicals analyst who attended a company meeting held a day after Reliance announced improved results for the financial year ended March 31, 1997.
The petrochemicals giant said on Tuesday its net profit climbed to 13.23 billion rupees ($370 million) in 1996/97 (April-March) from 13.05 billion in 1995/96.

In a presentation made to analysts late on Wednesday, Reliance said its 50 billion rupee petrochemicals complex in the western Indian state of Gujarat would be primarily financed through debt and internal accruals over the next three years.

Reliance raised $614 million through bond issues during 1996/97. The firm said in a written presentation it has so far raised international debt totalling $914 million with an average maturity of 23 years.
The company said its participation in the oil and gas sector acted as a hedge against the group's exposure in the petrochemical business and a depreciating Indian rupee.

Reliance said its investments in the Panna, Mukta and Tapti oil fields in western India would be in the range of $350 million over a period of more than five years. Capital expenditure incurred to date was 18 billion rupees.
The company expects annual revenues of 3.5 billion rupees by 1997/98 from these fields.
The petrochemicals giant said there was no material change in its product mix during 1996/97 over the previous year.
"Despite decrease in prices, operating margins (were) maintained due to volume growth and efficiency," Reliance said.
Operating profit margins climbed by 19 percent in 1996/97.
Analysts said Reliance had sidestepped higher taxes in the financial year ended March 31, 1997 by altering its method of calculating depreciation.
They said lower taxes contributed significantly to the improved net profit -- which was sharply above the consensus estimate of 12.06 billion rupees.
Reliance said taxation for the year worked out to 450 million rupees -- a mere 3.3 percent on profits against the 12.9 percent minimum alternate tax it was expected to pay.
"The lower tax is almost entirely because of the change in the firm's depreciation policy for its older plants," said another analyst who attended the meeting.

He said Reliance had switched to the written down value (WDV) method of calculating depreciation, from the straight line method (SLM), resulting in increased accumulated depreciation of 9.4 billion rupees from previous years.
"They have changed the method of calculating depreciation for all their older plants with retrospective effect resulting in sharply higher provisions for depreciation," he added. ($1 = 35.75 rupees)
